extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy/public finance; policymakers and historians of public finance
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter exposition on causes, methods, and consequences of public borrowing and debt in commercial and non-commercial states; explains creditor motives, instruments of borrowing, and institutional differences between countries. Useful as a conceptual framework for analyzing public debt formation and policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: War-induced necessity to borrow
rubrics_metrics.description: When war begins (or appears likely), immediate and great expense must be incurred for augmenting armies, fitting out fleets, and provisioning garrisoned towns; these expenses cannot wait for the slow returns of newly imposed taxes, so government has no other resource but borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the timing mismatch: revenue from new taxes may take ten or twelve months to reach the treasury, whereas war expenditures are immediate. War therefore forces governments into borrowing even if ordinary revenue equals ordinary expense in peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial society produces ability and inclination to lend
rubrics_metrics.description: A country abounding with merchants and manufacturers necessarily abounds with people whose capitals circulate frequently and who therefore have both the ability and inclination to lend to government on extraordinary occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchants' capitals circulate multiple times per year, enabling larger advances without diminishing trading capital; lending to government may even increase their trading capital by offering profitable transferable securities. This creates a ready market for public loans in commercial states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence in justice and property rights underpins public credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce and manufactures can seldom flourish without a regular administration of justice, security of property, faith of contracts, and confidence that the state will enforce payment of debts — the same confidence makes subjects willing to lend to government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions public credit as dependent on institutional trust: the justice of government and enforcement mechanisms create the basis for both ordinary commerce and extraordinary lending to the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rude (non-commercial) societies favor hoarding and sovereign saving
rubrics_metrics.description: In a rude state of society, individuals hoard and conceal money out of distrust of government and fear of plunder; few people can or will lend to government, so sovereigns must save to provide for extraordinary exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoarding served practical needs (flight, insecurity) and made borrowing impractical. Sovereign parsimony/saving is both natural and necessary in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government propensity to rely on borrowing when lenders are available
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments in commercial states are apt to repose on the ability and willingness of subjects to lend and therefore often dispense with the duty of saving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of credit tends to reduce governmental saving discipline: 'It foresees the facility of borrowing, and therefore dispenses itself from the duty of saving.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression of public debt instruments (personal credit → assigned funds → perpetual funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations generally begin borrowing on personal credit (no assigned fund), then borrow by assigning specific funds, and when that is insufficient move to perpetual funding (mortgaging funds in perpetuity to pay interest only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical progression explains how governments move from short anticipations to lasting funded debt; overloading funds or repeated anticipations make perpetual funding likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded debt components (first-kind and second-kind debts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfunded debt consists partly of debts that bear or are supposed to bear no interest (like arrears for extraordinary services) and partly of interest-bearing debts resembling private promissory notes (e.g., navy and exchequer bills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes composition of 'unfunded debt' with examples: arrears of services, navy/exchequer bills; notes role of Bank of England in discounting and circulating such bills to facilitate government borrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrowing by anticipation versus perpetual funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing by anticipation: taxes are anticipated for a short period (a year or a few years) with the fund expected to repay principal and interest within that time. Perpetual funding: taxes are rendered perpetual to pay interest only (a perpetual annuity), postponing repayment of principal indefinitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation could liberate public revenue after a few years if properly managed; perpetual funding raises larger sums immediately but likely delays indefinite liberation of revenue. Governments favor present relief, often at posterity's expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortgaging particular branches of revenue and the danger of overloading funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments sometimes assign or mortgage particular branches of public revenue for debt payment; repeated anticipation or overloading of such funds makes them insufficient to pay principal and interest and leads to funding for perpetuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (general mortgages/funds in England during 1697–1717) illustrate how successive prolongations and accumulations turned short-term anticipations into perpetual funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual funding preferred in exigencies despite long-term costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual funding can raise a greater immediate sum than anticipation; once accustomed to it, administrators prefer it because it relieves immediate exigencies even though it delays or eliminates future liberation of revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative observation: 'To relieve the present exigency, is always the object which principally interests those immediately concerned in the administration of public affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest rate reductions and creation/augmentation of a sinking fund
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductions in the market rate of interest (e.g., to five, then four, then 3.5–3 percent) reduced annuity costs and created a surplus in the produce of funds, forming a sinking fund intended for debt repayment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While instituted for payment of old debt, sinking funds can also facilitate contracting new debt because they serve as subsidiary funds that could be mortgaged in aid of other funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinking fund can facilitate contracting new debts (risk of misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sinking fund, though instituted to pay old debt, is a subsidiary fund always at hand that can be mortgaged to support new borrowing; this makes it paradoxically enable further indebtedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that the sinking fund's existence often aids in contracting more debt rather than eliminating it; historical practice shows ambiguous use of sinking funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate borrowing via annuities for terms and for lives (including tontines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments have borrowed by granting annuities for terms of years or for lives; annuities for lives may be granted on separate lives or in lots (tontines). These forms lie between short anticipations and perpetual funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical examples of term annuities and life annuities (e.g., 14% annuity for 16 years, exchanges into long-term annuities), and notes that annuities for long terms can be almost as valuable as perpetuities but are less attractive to purchasers who desire transferable stable stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tontines raise more money per revenue than separate-life annuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Annuities granted on lots of lives (tontines) can raise more money on the same revenue than annuities on separate lives because survivors succeed to deceased annuitants' annuities, increasing expected value to purchasers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains survivorship effect and why tontines are preferred where annuities are used: 'Upon the same revenue, more money can always be raised by tontines than by annuities for separate lives.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual annuities preferred by merchants for transferability and stable value
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants prefer perpetual annuities (redeemable by parliament) because their real value is stable and they make a more convenient transferable stock; annuities for lives or long terms lose value over time and are less liquid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains merchant incentives: they often intend to sell their subscriptions quickly, so prefer securities with steady value; annuities on one's own life or on another's life are less conveniently transferable and may sell at a loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/cultural composition of lenders shapes debt instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between countries (e.g., England vs France) in who lends — merchants vs financiers/farmers-general — lead to differences in the structure of public debt (England favors perpetual annuities; France has more life-annuities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that in France many lenders are wealthy, often bachelor bankers who don't care for posterity and thus prefer annuities for lives that end with them; in England the mercantile city makes merchants dominant lenders, who favor transferable perpetual annuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term annuities' marketability depends on purchaser motives
rubrics_metrics.description: An annuity for a long term of years, though intrinsically near equal in value to a perpetuity, will find fewer purchasers because people buying stock for family settlements or remote futurity avoid securities whose value continuously diminishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that subscribers who plan to sell prefer perpetual redeemable annuities to irredeemable long-term annuities; marketability, not intrinsic value alone, determines the choice of instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political stability and the presence of wealthy merchants support industry and credit
rubrics_metrics.description: The republican form of government (example: Holland) where owners of great capitals have influence supports industry and commerce because such owners accept lower returns in exchange for political respect and security; loss of that political status would drive capital away and harm commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Holland as a case: wealthy merchants tolerate lower profit to retain influence; if administration changes to nobles/soldiers and merchants lose importance, they would relocate their capital and residence, and industry would follow.
